channel.description: Half-hour teaching episodes for morning runs.

item.title: Wait, Did I Already Tell You That?
item.description: Wait, Did I Already Tell You That? Part one. The moment. You are partway into a story. Maybe it is at lunch with a colleague. Maybe it is on the couch with your wife after work. You are telling it well. You are just getting to the good part. And then you see it. A small smile. A polite nod that comes half a second too early. And they say, kindly, "Yeah, you told me." And you feel a little flush of embarrassment. Not a big one. Just enough to make you wonder. Why does this keep happening? Is it a memory thing? Is it a sign I talk too much? Is it because I share things so openly and so quickly...

item.title: Why We Wreck Good Things: Self-Sabotage, Small and Big
item.description: Why We Wreck Good Things: Self-Sabotage, Small and Big Part one. The question. A few days ago you said something out loud. You said, "Why do I like self sabotage so bad." And then you asked the bigger version. Why do people with a good life throw it away with one stupid decision? You know both versions. The small one looks like this. You have a free hour after work. You know the one thing that would actually move your life forward. And instead you tidy a drawer, check your phone, answer a text that could wait, and then the hour is gone. Nothing bad happened. Nothing good happened either. The...

item.title: Does nagging ever work? When the heart underneath wants to please
item.description: Does nagging ever work? When the heart underneath wants to please. Cold open. Picture yourself at fifteen. Your mom is asking, for the fourth time that week, about something. Homework, your room, church clothes, it doesn't matter what. And you are fighting it. Tooth and nail, as you put it. You roll your eyes, you stall, you argue. And yet, years later, here you are. You respect her. You respect your dad. And a lot of what they pushed on you, you now actually live. Now jump to your kitchen. You've asked your wife, more than once, to load the dishwasher a certain way. She pushed back. And then...

item.title: Rest in Hebrews, the rest that remains
item.description: Rest in Hebrews, the rest that remains Part one. A scene. Picture a Tuesday morning. You are up before it is light. You have read your Bible, and you have opened the planning chat, and you are texting a friend while the first answer is written. Everything on the list is reasonable. Every item is good. And somewhere in the middle of it, a small voice says, if I do all of this well, then I will finally be able to relax. Now picture the end of that same day. The list is mostly done. And you are not relaxed. A new list has quietly taken its place. That is the scene I want to start with, because...

item.title: Can I actually sit down and teach my kids? The 12 minute lesson
item.description: Part one. The question. Picture a normal morning in your room. It is about nine thirty. The kids came in at nine fifteen with breakfast. The morning sheet is on the desks. One kid is done the feelings grid and has drifted to the window. One kid has his hood up. One kid is asking you when break is, even though break is at ten twenty five, every day, no earlier and no later. And you are standing there with a question you typed into your phone half as a joke and half as a confession. "Is there a chance I can actually sit down and do a lesson with the kids and teach them things?" That question...

item.title: When a kid goes off, is there really nothing a teacher can do?
item.description: Cold open Picture a regular morning in your room. The taxis have dropped everyone off. Desk sheets are out. One student comes in already wound up. Maybe something happened at home, maybe in the taxi, maybe nothing you will ever know about. Within ten minutes he is swearing, the chair gets shoved, and another kid starts feeding it. You look over at your John Howard partner, and the thought that goes through your head is one you have heard in a lot of staff rooms. "There is nothing we can actually do. The system ties our hands." That is the question for today. You asked it like this: is it...

item.title: What a report card comment actually does for a struggling kid
item.description: Picture this. It's a weeknight in late January. You're at the kitchen table with your laptop, and your wife has gone to bed. You've got a student's mark in one box, the six learning skills in a row of little drop downs, and an empty comment box staring back at you. You paste your notes into the AI. It hands you back a paragraph that is, honestly, pretty good. It's accurate. It sounds like a teacher. And a small voice in your head says: why am I even doing this? Who reads this? Does this help this kid at all, or am I just feeding the machine because the job says I have to? That's the question...

item.title: Authority Without the Standoff
item.description: Picture a kitchen in your hometown. You're small. There's a mess on the floor, maybe toys, maybe a spilled bowl of cereal, and you want your mom to clean it up. She won't. She says something like, "You made it, you clean it." And you lose it. You kick, you scream, you tell her she's being totally unreasonable. Now fast forward. You're grown up, and you look back on that, and two things are true at once. One, she was right. She was holding a principle, and it was a good one. Two, it was also a bit much. There's a version of that afternoon where nobody had to dig in their heels at all. That's...

item.title: Undivided Devotion, for a Married Man with a Full Calendar
item.description: Undivided Devotion: One Heart, A Full Calendar Picture a Tuesday. You wake up early, you sit with your Bible, you pray with your wife. Then it's the classroom by nine fifteen, breakfast and the morning sheet, the first break at ten twenty five exactly. Then the drive, maybe IO, maybe a stop at the hardware store. Then home for an hour. Then MC. Then home again, late, and your wife is tired, and you're tired, and the day is done. Every single thing on that list is good. Not one of them is sin. And yet you can get to the end of a day like that and feel like you were never fully anywhere. Your...

item.title: Slow to Anger, Steady in Body
item.description: Slow to Anger, Steady in Body: Practicing Calm Because of God Picture a weekday morning in your classroom. It's the second block. You've just finished explaining the task, and a student, call him J, pushes his chair back, says something sharp under his breath, and looks right at you to see what you'll do. Everyone else looks too. In that half second, your body has already started to answer. Your jaw tightens. Your shoulders come up. Your breath goes shallow and high. Your voice is loading a reply that's a little louder and a little faster than you'd choose. Now picture the same moment, but...

item.title: Grace That Doesn't Slide (when "it's OK today" becomes a pattern)
item.description: Grace That Doesn't Slide It's a weekday morning in your classroom. The desk sheet is out. Someone comes in, drops into a chair, puts their hood up, and lays their head down on their arms. You look at them and you can tell they're wiped. Maybe they worked late. Maybe home was loud. Maybe they just didn't sleep. And you think, okay, today, you need it. Rest. It's fine. That felt kind. And honestly, it might have been the right call that day. But then the next day, same chair, same hood, same head on the desk. And the day after that. And now there are two heads down instead of one. And you're...

item.title: Stand Like a Martial Artist, Body Language for When Someone Yells
item.description: Stand Like a Martial Artist, Body Language for Staying Steady When Someone Yells COLD OPEN Picture this. You are in the grocery store on a Saturday. Your wife is two aisles over. You reach for something on a shelf and a man behind you, a total stranger, decides you were in his way. He starts yelling. His face is red. He is closer than you would like. People are looking. Now picture a different room. It is a Tuesday in your classroom. One of your students is upset. Maybe it is about the work, maybe it is about something that happened at home last night. Their voice is going up. They are...

item.title: Why Airing Our Dirty Laundry Feels So Good
item.description: Listen: Why Airing Our Dirty Laundry Feels So Good Picture the end of a long day. The bell has gone, the room is finally quiet, and a colleague leans on your doorframe and says, "Can I just tell you about my afternoon?" And then it comes out. The student who would not stop. The email from the office. The thing someone said in the meeting. And you jump in with your own. Ten minutes later you are both laughing, shaking your heads, and you walk to the parking lot feeling lighter. Or it is the evening at home. Something happened today that bugged you, and you get to finally say it out loud to...

item.title: How lobbying actually works in Canada
item.description: It's a Tuesday in your Civics and Careers class. You've got a news story up on the screen about some new government rule. Maybe it's about trucking, or farming, or vaping. And one of your kids, slouched at the back, says what half the class is thinking. It doesn't matter what we think. Rich companies just pay off the politicians. That's how it works. And part of you wants to say, no, that's not how it works. But another part of you isn't totally sure. You've heard the word lobbyist your whole life. It sounds a bit shady. Men in suits in Ottawa, handing over envelopes. And you realize you...

item.title: How much money do you need to stop worrying about spending?
item.description: It's Saturday morning, and you're scrolling Marketplace with your coffee. And there it is. A set of winter tires for the truck, right size, good tread, a fair price. Four hundred dollars. You've been meaning to get winter tires for weeks. And something happens in your chest. You open the banking app. You look at the balance. You do some math in your head. The mortgage comes out on the first. There's the phone bill. Christmas is coming. And you hover over the message button. And you put the phone down. And you pick it up again. Now here's the strange part. You can afford the tires. You know...

item.title: One sentence for when small tasks feel heavy. What the research says about self talk
item.description: It's Thursday night, around eight. Supper's done. And there's a handful of small jobs waiting. Upload the marks for one class. Answer two emails. Put the laundry away. Reply to the guy on Marketplace who wants to come look at the snowblower. Top up the washer fluid in the truck. None of them is hard. Most would take five minutes. Some would take one. And yet each one feels like lifting an engine block. You look at the laptop, and something in your chest sinks. You look at the laundry basket, and you sit back down. And there's a voice in your head, running a little commentary. Ugh. I can't be...

item.title: Getting a stubborn kid across the line. The reluctant student, and the kid who won't go out
item.description: It's Monday in your construction class. Everyone has a hammer and a pile of two by fours. The job today is simple. Frame a small wall section. And there's one kid at the back bench, arms crossed, hood up, the hammer sitting untouched. You walk over. Come on, let's go. He says, this is stupid. You say, it's part of the course. He says, I don't care. And you can feel the next ten minutes coming. You push. He digs in. You push harder. He digs in harder. And by the end of class, the wall is still a pile of lumber, and you're both a little angrier than when you started. Now picture a different...

item.title: The ignored laws, part three. How Christ fulfils the law, and what that means on a Tuesday
item.description: It's Tuesday. You were up at five thirty for devotions. You read, you prayed, you meant it. Then the day happened. The truck took three tries to start. You got to school late and flustered. And in second period, a kid in your Shifting Gears class said something rude under his breath, the same thing he's said a dozen times, and this time you snapped. Not a disaster. But louder and sharper than you wanted, in front of the class. You saw his face close up like a door. That evening, driving home, two voices start talking in your head. The first voice says, you call yourself a Christian? You did...

item.title: The ignored laws, part two. The strangest laws, and what they meant
item.description: It's the start of a new term in your construction class. You're giving the safety tour. You get to the yellow cabinet in the corner, the one for flammables. And you explain that the gas for the small engines goes in here, and the cleaning chemicals go over there, in a different cabinet, and they never share a shelf. One of the new kids rolls his eyes. Why does it matter? It's all just stuff in bottles. And you know the answer. Some things are fine on their own and dangerous together. The rule looks fussy to a kid who doesn't know chemistry. To you, it's obvious. The rule is the knowledge,...

item.title: Influence in the classroom, part two. Getting the truth from a student
item.description: It's last period on a Thursday. You walk into the shop after a short trip to the office, and something's wrong. There's a fresh gouge in the bench top. Someone has been playing with the router. It wasn't there twenty minutes ago. Four kids were in the room. Three of them look at you normally. The fourth, Tyler, is suddenly very interested in his phone. You feel the hunch land in your gut. It was him. You can feel the words lining up in your mouth. Tyler. I know it was you. Just admit it. And you know what happens next, because it's happened before. He says, it wasn't me. You say, come on. He...

item.title: Open loops, part four. One loop at a time
item.description: It's Wednesday evening, and you're standing in the garage. Look around. On the bench, the uprights for the new shelving, cut two weeks ago, still waiting for the shelves. On the floor, the box with the truck part, opened, not installed. In the corner, three things you photographed for Marketplace, but never actually listed. And on the workbench, a stack of marking you carried out here because you thought you might do a bit while the glue dried, except there's no glue drying, because the shelving isn't glued yet. You've been busy. Really busy. You've been working on all of it. And none of it...

item.title: Open loops, part three. Why the calendar makes things happen
item.description: It's Sunday night, around nine thirty. The kids are in bed. You're on the couch, a little tired, thinking about the week. And you make some promises to yourself. Tomorrow I'll get up and run before school. This week I'll call that parent I've been meaning to call. This week I'll finally start on the shelving in the garage. Good intentions. Real ones. You mean every word. Then Monday morning comes. The alarm goes. It's dark. It's cold. The bed is warm. And a little voice says, let's think about this. Do I really need to run today? I could run after school. I could run tomorrow. And by the time...

item.title: Open loops, part two. The task fills the time you give it
item.description: It's a Saturday in the fall. You've got nothing on the calendar. No games, no church thing, no visitors. And there's one job on the list. Brake pads on the truck. So you tell yourself, great, I've got the whole day for that. And somehow, the whole day goes to the brake pads. You have a slow coffee. You watch a video on the job, then a second video, because the first guy did it differently. You go looking for the right socket. You decide the garage needs sweeping before you start. You make a run to the parts store for something you probably didn't need. By four in the afternoon the pads are...

item.title: The psychology of hosting
item.description: It is Thursday night. Small group is at your place. The house is clean, mostly. The coffee is on. There is a plate of something on the counter. At five to seven the first car pulls in, and it is the couple you know well, and that part is easy. Then at ten past seven the doorbell goes again, and it is the new couple from church. You met them once in the foyer. You said, you should come out on Thursday. And they did. They are standing on your porch holding a bag of chips they bought on the way. They do not know where to put their shoes. They do not know who anyone is. And you are in the...

item.title: The ignored laws, part one. Every law has a reason
item.description: Picture your construction class on a job. Maybe it's a deck. One of your guys is up on the frame, and he's annoyed. He wants to know why you're making him put a railing on something that's barely off the ground. He says nobody's going to fall. He says the inspector won't even look. And you say what every builder eventually says. The railing isn't for today. The railing is for the night of the barbecue, when somebody's uncle backs up with a plate in his hand and doesn't know where the edge is. Now here's the thing. God wrote that exact law. Three thousand years ago, in the book of Deuteronomy,...

item.title: The AI temptation for teachers
item.description: It is Sunday night. The house is quiet. You have your laptop open at the kitchen table and a list of what Monday needs. A desk sheet. A rubric for the deck project in your construction class. Something for Civics on how a bill becomes law. You type one sentence into the chat box. Forty seconds later you have a rubric. Four levels, clean language, nicely formatted. Honestly, it is better looking than the one you made two years ago by hand. And you feel two things at once. The first is relief. That is twenty minutes back. Maybe you get to bed before ten. The second is harder to name. It is a...

item.title: Open loops, part one. Why unfinished things nag at you
item.description: It's Saturday morning. You're in the driveway, standing beside the truck. The hood is up. The new part is sitting on the fender, still in the box. You got halfway last weekend, then the light went, then the week happened. And all week, at the strangest moments, that truck showed up in your head. In the middle of a lesson. At the red light. At night, right when you were about to fall asleep. Not loudly. Just a little tap on the shoulder. Hey. Remember me. I'm not done. And it isn't only the truck. There's a stack of marking in your bag that you started and didn't finish. There's a Marketplace...

item.title: Influence in the classroom, part one. Framing, anchoring and authority
item.description: It's second period, in your construction class. A kid I'll call Tyler is slumped at the bench with his hood up. The worksheet for the shed plan is in front of him, face down. You walk over. You've got options. You could say, "Tyler, are you going to do this today?" You already know how that ends. He says no, and now you're in a standoff. Or you could crouch down and say, "Do you want to start with the materials list or the measurements?" He shrugs. Then he flips the sheet over and points at the materials list. It worked. And a small voice in the back of your head asks a fair question. Did I...

item.title: The forgetting curve and retrieval practice
item.description: It's Monday morning. Your class is settling in. Someone is still eating a granola bar. Someone else has their hood up and their head down. Last Thursday, you taught a good lesson in Civics. It went well. They were with you. You talked about the three levels of government, and who handles what. A kid even made a joke about the mayor fixing potholes, and everyone laughed. You walked out of that room thinking, they got it. So now you ask a simple question. Which level of government runs the schools in Ontario? Silence. A shrug. One student says, the mayor? Another says, the prime minister. The...

item.title: Teenage sleep and the shifted body clock
item.description: Picture first period. It is a grey Tuesday in November. You have been up since five thirty. You have read your Bible, prayed, had your coffee, and you are ready. The room is not. One kid has his hood up and his head on the desk. Another is staring at the wall like the wall owes her money. A third walked in eleven minutes late with an energy drink and no explanation. You say good morning. Two people grunt. And somewhere in the back of your mind a voice says, these kids just don't care. Hold that thought. Because by the end of this run, I want you to hear a different voice. Here is the promise...

item.title: Switching off after school
item.description: It is eight o'clock on a Tuesday night. The kids are in bed or close to it. You are standing at the sink with your hands in warm water, rinsing a pot. And you are not at the sink. Not really. You are back in your classroom at two fifteen. A student is leaning back in his chair, smirking, saying the thing he knows will land. You can hear his exact words. You can hear what you said back. And now, six hours later, you are rewriting your answer. You are saying the better line. The calmer line. The line that would have ended it. The pot is clean. You have been rinsing it for a while. Your wife...

item.title: How long a habit really takes
item.description: It is five thirty in the morning. The house is dark and quiet. You come down the stairs, and you do not stop to think about where to go. Your feet take you to the same chair. Your hand finds the same lamp. The Bible is where you left it yesterday. The coffee is started before you have fully woken up. Now think about something different. Think about a Tuesday in September, the second week of school. You told your Shifting Gears students that every morning starts with the desk sheet. You said it clearly. You put it on the board. And still, half the room walks in, drops their bag, and pulls out...

item.title: Defaults and paying yourself first
item.description: It's a Thursday night. Payday was this morning. You open the banking app on the couch, and the chequing account looks healthy. Fuller than usual. You think, good, this month I'll put some away. Maybe a few hundred dollars into the tax free savings account. You'll do it this weekend, once the bills settle. Then the weekend comes. There's a birthday gift to buy. The car needs tires soon. Someone suggests takeout. None of it is wasteful. All of it is reasonable. And by the next payday, the money you meant to save is simply gone. Not spent on anything foolish. Just spent. Now here's the strange...
